div.head:
No. 917
Department of State Position Paper
div.p:
Confidential
SD/A/C.1/447/Rev. 1
United Nations Relief And Works Agency For Palestine (Unrwa): Reports Of The Director And Advisory Commission
The Problem

The Report of the Director and the special joint report of the Director and the Advisory Commission of UNRWA will be before the Ad Hoc Political Committee for debate and will involve the following questions:

list.item: 1. The extension of the life of UNRWA.

2. Other substantive issues raised in the report and contained in the report’s recommendations for a General Assembly resolution including the budget for continued relief and for the reintegration program.
3. The injection into the committee’s debate of certain other political issues involved in the Palestine question.

div.p: United States Position

1. The United States will support the continuation of UNRWA for a period of five years as necessary for the welfare of the Arab refugees. This position is consistent with United States objectives in the area, and with the objectives of the Mutual Security Act of 1954 and the explicit positions of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee (See “comment” for citations).
2. With regard to the substantive issues raised in the report, the United States will hold:

list.item: a. On compensation or repatriation, the failure to resolve these problems must not be an obstacle to UNRWA’s efforts to rehabilitate refugees as promptly as possible.

b. Any redefinition of a refugee eligible for relief will be contingent on the establishment of an effective system for determining the bona fides of relief recipients and the deletion from the registration rolls of persons not entitled to relief.

c. No specific authorization to the Director to employ a portion of rehabilitation funds for general economic development programs of the area governments is desirable or necessary. Rehabilitation funds are to ensure to the extent practicable the settlement of the refugee question and UNRWA already has adequate terms of reference under previous General Assembly resolutions so that funds can be spent in the manner and for purposes designed to achieve the Agency’s objective.
d. The budgets for relief and for rehabilitation are approved.

div.p: 3. It opposes the injection of any political issues, not raised by the reports but involved in the Palestine question, into the draft resolution of UNRWA. Specifically these issues might relate to duties and functions of the Palestine Conciliation Commission (PCC); the enforcement of previous United Nations resolutions; territorial and boundary adjustments; and the status of Jerusalem. Specific instructions from the Department should be sought by the Delegation should any such issues become the subject of a draft resolution.
4. It will inititate, if necessary, and seek limited co-sponsorship of well-disposed nations for the draft resolution attached.
Comment

A. There are two aspects of the Arab refugee problem: relief and eventual resettlement. Both the immediate problem of relief and the long-range preparations for the resettlement of the refugees require the continued earnest interest of the United States and the continuance in existence of the UNRWA, the agency presently handling these problems. The question of the agency’s continued existence will come before the General Assembly this year. Because the refugee problem has not been solved and no better means of settling it is likely to be found than such an organization as UNRWA, the United States should support the continuation of the agency and its activities. This position is consistent with that set forth in the report of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, No. 1799, dated July 13, 1954, on the Mutual Security Act of 1954.

“Economic and political factors have been the major blocks to a vigorous reintegration program. The economic factors revolve mostly around the poverty and aridity of the area and could be solved in part by the regional development of water resources proposed under the TVA plan. Thus far, political factors have prevented the acceptance of this plan by the nations concerned. The committee cannot express too strongly its deep concern over the political tensions in the Near East, and its conviction that the problem is one for the United Nations. The United States should continue to cooperate with the U.N. in seeking a solution even though some years may be required to find it.” (Page 40)
Excerpt from Report of the Committee on Foreign Affairs on the Mutual Security Act of 1954 (Report No. 1925, Part I).

“The countries involved are dry and barren and the lack of full cooperation on the part of some of the governments involved, as well as the refugees themselves, has been a contributing factor in the slow progress in this field.

“Nevertheless, the United States regards the tension in the Near East as of serious concern. It is important to indicate by authorizing
funds even before appropriations are to be requested that the United States desires to cooperate in finding a solution to the problem.

“An authorization is made of $30 million for Fiscal Year 1955, but appropriation for this amount is not being sought in this session of Congress. The unobligated Fiscal Year 1954 funds, presently estimated at $29 million is authorized to be reappropriated.” (Page 72)

B. The report which will be before the Ad Hoc Committee is not an “agreed” report although drafted by the members of the Advisory Commission and approved by them ad referendum it has been signed by the United States with reservations and has not been signed by Jordan or Syria. The reservations of the United States was contained in a memorandum which was circulated to the members of the Advisory Commission (see attachment). This statement in the memorandum should be part of the United States Representative’s speech in the Ad Hoc Committee. Because the report is not agreed to, particularly by two of the Arab members of the Advisory Commission, we may expect that the debate will be far more acrimonious than would have been the case had the report obtained the signatures of all of the members of the Advisory Commission. For a discussion of tactics in debate see Item 2 below.
C. The Advisory Commission’s report may be summarized as follows:

1. It indicates dissatisfaction with the small progress which has been made in the settlement of the refugee problem, particularly in the matters of repatriation and compensation. (For your information: It has been long since agreed by Arab Delegations that rehabilitation need not prejudice the other rights of refugees.) It suggests coordination between the Advisory Commission and PCC.

2. It suggests that UNRWA’s mandate be continued for another five years. It discusses the fact that while progress has been made on surveys for major projects in connection with the resettlement of refugees the existing economic and political circumstances and the prospects for new projects do not promise an early resettlement of the refugees. It accordingly suggests that while it is important to find new projects the Director should be authorized and given discretion over a portion of the rehabilitation fund for the purpose to permit the Agency to participate in general development programs of the Governments of the area. It goes on to point out that such general development programs will require substantial capital funds in addition to those which could be made available through the Agency. (For your information: Such funds have been available in past years and will be sought again by the Executuve Branch of the government.) It also stresses the importance of the education and vocational training programs as part of the rehabilitation of the Agency.

3. With regard to the relief program it suggests that the definition of a refugee should be revised to include certain refugees not
now eligible by the definition. It also points out that a substantial number of children of refugees do not receive rations at the present time and suggests procedures whereby these problems might be handled.

4. While believing that present standards of relief are adequate it suggests that there is a distinct need for supplementing present contributions of clothing with a distribution of cotton cloth particularly for use in making children’s garments.
5. It indicates that it believes to be necessary budgetary requirements for the forthcoming year.

D. The Palestine question has many facets of which the refugee problem is only one. Other aspects of the problem include the question of a peace settlement between Israel and the Arab States, the settlement of the question of status of Jerusalem, and the improvement of the general economic and security situation in the area. The unhappy tendency in General Assembly debate on any phase of this problem is for a number of delegations, particularly the Arabs, to make reference to aspects of the problem other than the one technically the subject of discussion. Thus it may be expected that in the forthcoming debate the question of Israel repatriating the Arab refugees, Israel’s paying compensation to the refugees, Israel’s agreeing to accept the 1947 partitioning resolution as the basis for a political settlement, all will be raised by the Arabs. The Israelis in retort will make proposals for direct negotiations with the Arabs which are quite unacceptable to them. The fact that our new Ambassador to Israel presented his credentials to the Israeli President in Jerusalem will be attacked not only by the Arabs but possibly by a number of the Latin American countries in prejudicing the United Nations position on the internationalization of Jerusalem. With regard to the security situation in the area comments may be forthcoming and our arms aid programs for several of the Arab States may be subject to Israeli attack. The earnest efforts of the United States Delegation should be directed to avoiding acrimonious discussion of these questions which are peripheral to the debate on the Advisory Commission’s report. It is our present understanding that the Director of UNRWA, Mr. Harry Labouisse, in his opening statement will urge that the debate be limited to discussion of the report. The United States Delegation should support this position.

E. With regard to the various problems referred to above as likely to arise in debate it is of utmost importance that the United States Delegation bear in mind the importance of avoiding anything in debate or in a resolution arising out of the debate which might prejudice the further negotiations which Ambassador Johnston will be undertaking with the Arab States and Israel commencing in January 1955. It is the Department’s view that an international
agreement for the mutual development of the Jordan Valley may well be realized as a result of Ambassador Johnston’s projected negotiations. Such an agreement on this project would be the most significant step which the states in the area could take toward an eventual settlement of all of the problems involved in the Palestine question. While supporting this and other similar programs the United States Delegation should avoid anything which might prejudice the achievement of such an agreement. However, this does not mean that the Arab Delegations and Israel cannot be dealt with frankly and firmly in any discussions which the United States Delegation may have with them.

The debate on the Palestine refugee question inevitably is time consuming. This is due to the facts that: (a) there are two consistent Arab trouble makers in any debate on this question, Ahmed Shukairi, Assistant Secretary General of the Arab League and acting head of the Syrian Delegation (in violation of Arab League directives), and Dr. Fadil Al Jamali, head of the Iraqi Delegation; (b) all the Arab Delegations and Israel will insist on long speeches on the subject; (c) there is a general lack of understanding of the problem on the part of many [of] the delegations, but a willingness to appear as mediators in debate, particularly as its temper rises. Dr. Jamali and Mr. Shukairi are old hands at debate on this question and they may be expected to produce several long speeches each on the subject. These speeches will probably be counterproductive to their cause and if allowed to proceed unimpeded will tend to induce a healthy attitude of moderation on the part of other Arab Delegations and an irritated and aloof attitude on the part of other delegations which might normally wish to participate in debate. Accordingly, the United States Delegation should not interfere with Dr. Jamali and Mr. Shukairi’s free reign in debate. The United States Delegation should be prepared, after an appropriate time following the speeches of the Arab States and Israel, to deliver a moderate conciliatory but frank discussion of the problem. It should be prepared to initiate, if necessary, the attached draft resolution with appropriate co-sponsors. It should seek to discourage resolutions or amendments to the attached draft resolution which tend to discuss subjects not the subject of debate. It should seek instructions if it becomes necessary to vote on any such resolutions or amendments.
[Attachment]
Draft Resolution
The General Assembly,

Recalling its resolutions 194 (III) of 11 December 1948; 302 (IV) of 8 December 1949; 393 (V) of 2 December 1950; 513 (VI) of 26 January 1952; 614 (VII) of 6 November 1952; and 720 (VIII) of 27 November 1953;
Decides to extend the mandate of the Agency for five years ending 30 June 1960;

Requests the Director, in consultation with the Advisory Commission, to continue negotiations with the governments of the host countries with a view to arranging the gradual transfer to them of the administration of relief during the five year period;

Requests the governments of the area to continue to cooperate with the Director in carrying out presently agreed projects and, further, to cooperate in the search for new projects capable of supporting substantial numbers of refugees, and in reaching agreement thereon;
Decides to maintain the rehabilitation fund of $200,000,000, subject to reductions for expenditures already made;
Requests the Negotiating Committee for Extra-Budgetary Funds after consultation with the Director of UNRWA to seek such funds as may be required by the Agency, from time to time.

note.p: For instruction of the U.S. Delegation to the Ninth Regular Session of the General Assembly. An earlier version of this paper, SD/A/C.1/447, was dated Sept. 11. (IO files, lot 71 D 440)
The report of the director of UNRWA to the Ninth Session of the General Assembly covered the period from July 1, 1953 to June 30, 1954. (U.N. doc. A/2717)

On Nov. 23, France, Turkey, the United Kingdom, and the United States submitted a joint draft resolution (U.N. doc. A/AC.76/L.15) based on the recommendations of the joint report of the Director and Advisory Commission of UNRWA. This draft resolution was adopted by the Ad Hoc Political Committee on Nov 30 by 41 votes to none, with 8 abstentions; it was adopted by the General Assembly on Dec. 4 as Resolution 818 (IX), the text of which is printed as Document 926.
